blocks.title: Modeling
blocks.body:
The modeling stage is where data becomes intelligence - and where the ethical properties of the AI system begin to take shape. Choices made here, such as which features to include, how to weight different outcomes, and what to optimise for, all carry ethical consequences.

This is also the stage where bias can emerge or be amplified, and where the tools of responsible AI - explainability, documentation and security testing - are most directly applied.

blocks.title: If you use AI tools rather than build them
blocks.body: You won't be testing a model's performance across demographic groups or writing its model card - the vendor should have done that already. But knowing these are the checks a responsible developer runs turns them into fair questions you can ask: does this tool have a model card? Has its performance been tested across the groups it's actually used with? That's a reasonable thing to ask of any AI vendor - including the one your own organisation already uses.

blocks.title: The frameworks suggest...
blocks.body:
The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity - and to be sufficiently transparent that deployers can understand and oversee their operation.

ISO/IEC 42001 requires that AI systems be evaluated against defined performance criteria, with documentation of known limitations and risks - including records that allow the system's behaviour to be explained and audited, before and after deployment.

items.title: Why explainability matters
items.body: When an AI system makes or influences a decision that affects a person - whether they receive a loan, a job interview, or a medical diagnosis - that person has a legitimate interest in understanding why. Explainability is not just a technical goal - it is an ethical expectation across the board, and a legal requirement in specific contexts: UK GDPR and the EU GDPR give people a right to meaningful information about the logic involved in solely automated decisions that significantly affect them, and the EU AI Act imposes transparency duties on high-risk systems, including a right to explanation of individual decisions under Article 86.
items.graphicAlt: A magnifying glass inspecting a document, representing scrutinising a decision

items.title: Types of explainability
items.body: Global explainability helps us understand how the model behaves overall - which features it weighs most heavily. Local explainability helps us understand why the model made a specific decision in a specific case. Both matter for responsible AI, serving different stakeholders.
items.graphicAlt: A large outlined circle (the overall model) containing a smaller solid circle (one specific decision)

items.title: Explainable AI (XAI) tools
items.body: Tools such as LIME, SHAP and counterfactual explanations are designed to make AI reasoning interpretable to humans. They translate complex model outputs into language that can be understood, challenged and acted upon - by developers, decision-makers and those affected.
items.graphicAlt: A cog, representing the tools used to inspect how a model works

items.title: Ask yourself
items.body:
• Could you explain to someone why your AI made the decision it did about them?
  • Are there groups for whom the AI's reasoning is less well understood?
  • What would you do if an AI decision appeared wrong or unfair?
items.graphicAlt: A question mark in a circle

items.title: Fairness by design
items.body: Fairness isn't only something to test for once a model already exists - it can be built in during training. Techniques include re-weighting or resampling underrepresented groups beforehand (pre-processing), adding fairness constraints directly to the training objective (in-processing), and adjusting a trained model's outputs to correct for measured disparities (post-processing). Deciding which groups to protect, and which definition of fairness to optimise for, is an ethical choice as much as a technical one - the same tension the COMPAS case study raises. Common definitions include demographic parity (each group receives positive outcomes at the same rate), equalised odds (error rates are balanced across groups), and calibration (a given score means the same thing regardless of group) - as the COMPAS case study shows, satisfying one can mean violating another.

items.title: Testing for bias
items.body: Before deployment, AI models should be tested not only for overall accuracy but for differential performance across groups. A model that is 90% accurate overall may be significantly less accurate for minority groups - a pattern that must be detected and addressed before the model goes live.

items.title: Model cards
items.body: Model cards are structured documents describing an AI model's intended use, performance across demographic groups, known limitations and ethical considerations. Originally proposed by Google researchers, they are now a widely adopted best practice for transparent AI documentation.

items.title: AI security testing
items.body: AI systems face specific security risks: adversarial attacks (inputs designed to fool the model), data poisoning (corrupting training data), model inversion (reconstructing representative inputs or attributes from a trained model), membership inference (determining whether a specific individual's data was in the training set) and training data extraction (recovering verbatim training examples, including personal data, directly from a model's outputs). Security testing is an important and often overlooked component of responsible development.

items.title: Generative AI and LLM-specific risks
items.body: Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) introduce risks that don't map neatly onto the security concerns above. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 - an industry-standard reference, updated as new risks emerge - ranks prompt injection (LLM01: getting a model to follow hidden or disguised instructions instead of its intended ones) as the single most significant LLM risk, followed by sensitive information disclosure (LLM02: a model revealing training data, or another user's data, in its responses). Further down the same list, it also names excessive agency (LLM06: an AI agent taking actions beyond what it was actually authorised to do, exactly what happened in the case study covered later in this course) and misinformation (LLM09: a model confidently generating false information, often called 'hallucination', that then drives flawed decisions). See the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for the current full list, and the separate OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for risks specific to autonomous agents like the one in the Replit case study.

items.title: Generative AI's ethical questions beyond security
items.body: Not every generative AI concern is a security risk to test for - some are ethical questions in their own right. Hallucination isn't just a security weakness; a model confidently inventing facts, citations or code that don't exist causes real harm whenever someone trusts it, security incident or not. Copyright and intellectual property questions run in both directions - what a model was trained on, and who owns what it then generates. Deepfakes and disinformation - synthetic media convincing enough to pass as real - raise questions of consent, harm and trust in what we see and hear. Many jurisdictions are introducing AI content labelling requirements for exactly this reason, such as the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations. And there's a subtler cost: over-reliance and deskilling, where routinely accepting AI output erodes the judgement needed to catch it when the output is wrong - covered in more detail on the Using Copilot Responsibly page.

items.title: Environmental impact
items.body: Training and running large AI models consumes significant energy and water for data centre cooling, and contributes to electronic waste from specialised hardware. Independent estimates put the training of OpenAI's GPT-3 alone at around 552 tonnes of CO2 equivalent; larger, more capable models are estimated to run considerably higher, though AI companies rarely disclose exact figures - itself a transparency gap. The EU's Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI and UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI both name environmental sustainability as a core requirement of ethical AI, not a side effect to overlook - a model's environmental footprint is a legitimate factor to weigh against its benefits, alongside more familiar concerns like accuracy and fairness.

items.title: Implementation tips
items.body:
• Consider fairness constraints as a design input, not just a post-hoc test - re-weighting, in-processing constraints or output adjustment may all be options depending on your model type.
  • Test performance separately for different demographic groups - not just overall accuracy.
  • Produce a model card documenting limitations and ethical considerations before deployment.
  • Include security testing as a standard part of your development process, not an afterthought.
  • Set a threshold for acceptable differential performance - and don't deploy until it's met.
  • Weigh a model's compute, energy and environmental footprint against its benefits - and prefer a smaller or more efficient model when it meets the need just as well.

blocks.title: Case study: Facial analysis and bias
blocks.body:
A 2018 study by MIT researcher Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru, Gender Shades, examined commercial facial analysis (gender classification) systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ - software that infers a person's gender from their face, not systems that identify who they are. All three systems performed significantly worse on darker-skinned faces - and worst of all on darker-skinned women, with error rates up to 34 percentage points higher than for lighter-skinned men.

The researchers had no access to the vendors' training data, so they couldn't confirm directly what it contained - but the benchmark datasets they analysed were heavily skewed towards lighter-skinned faces, and the error pattern this produced is consistent with training and benchmark data likely dominated by lighter-skinned faces. The bias was not a programming error - it was a direct consequence of unrepresentative data and a failure to test for differential performance before deployment.

Source: Buolamwini & Gebru, Gender Shades (2018)

blocks.title: What testing approach would have caught this bias in the facial analysis systems before deployment?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: Switching to a more advanced algorithm that achieved a higher score for overall accuracy.
items.feedback: Not quite. A higher overall accuracy score can still hide large gaps between groups - these systems could well have scored 'accurate' overall while still failing badly for darker-skinned women.

items.text: Simply collecting a much larger volume of training images before building the model.
items.feedback: Not quite. More images alone don't fix the problem if the new images are drawn from the same unrepresentative sources as before - what matters is who's represented, not just the volume.

items.text: Testing the model's performance separately across demographic groups, not just overall accuracy.
Training the model on synthetic images instead of real photographs of real people.
items.feedback: Not quite. Synthetic data isn't a fix by default - it can still encode the same biases as the real data it was generated from, unless that's specifically corrected for.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The bias was detectable through disaggregated testing - breaking down performance metrics by demographic group. Testing for overall accuracy alone would have missed the problem. Responsible AI requires differential testing across the groups a model will be applied to, before deployment.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The bias was detectable through disaggregated testing - breaking down performance by demographic group. Overall accuracy alone would have missed it. This is why responsible AI requires differential testing across all groups a model will be applied to.

blocks.title: Coming up...
blocks.body: Once an AI system is built and tested, the work of responsible AI enters a new phase. In Deployment and Beyond, we'll look at monitoring AI systems in the real world, governing their use, and ensuring accountability over time.
